lesson.title: How compound interest works
lesson.summary: See why money grows faster over time when interest earns interest.
lesson.objective: Calculate compound growth year by year and explain why starting early matters.

hook.prompt: You invest $1,000 at 10% a year and leave it alone. About how much do you have after 7 years?
hook.explanation: Each year's interest joins the balance, so the next year earns interest on a bigger amount: about $1,949 after 7 years.

options.feedback: That adds $100 seven times. It misses the interest earned on earlier interest.
That would take 100% a year, not 10%.

bricks.title: Interest on interest
bricks.body: With **compound interest**, each year's interest is added to your balance. Next year you earn interest on that bigger balance, so growth speeds up over time.

term.definition: The amount you start with, written \( P \).

bricks.prompt: $1,000 at 5% a year, compounded yearly. How much after 2 years?
bricks.hint: Work out year 1 first, then use that as the new starting amount.
bricks.explanation:
Each year's interest joins the balance, so year 2 earns interest on $1,050.
Year 1: $1,000 × 1.05 = $1,050
Year 2: $1,050 × 1.05 = $1,102.50

options.feedback: That's simple interest. Year 2 also earns interest on year 1's $50.
That's after 1 year. Apply the 5% growth once more.
That's 0.5% a year. 5% is 0.05, so multiply by 1.05.

bricks.prompt: Fill in the growth factor for a 5% rate.
bricks.explanation: Multiplying by 1.05 keeps 100% of the balance and adds 5%.

mistakes.feedback: 0.05 gives only the interest ($50). Multiply by 1.05 to keep the original $1,000 too.
1.5 would be 50% growth. 5% is 0.05, so the factor is 1.05.

bricks.title: Time does the heavy lifting
bricks.body: Compounding is slow at first and fast later. The **rule of 72** estimates doubling time: 72 ÷ rate = years. At 7%, money doubles about every 10 years, so the third decade adds more than the first two combined.

bricks.prompt: Using the rule of 72, about how many years does money take to double at 6%?

options.feedback: That's the rate itself. Divide 72 by the rate instead.
72 is the rule's constant. Divide it by the rate, 6.

bricks.prompt: Both earn 7% a year. Who has more at age 65?
bricks.explanation: Ana ends with about $252,000 and Ben with about $227,000. Starting early beats putting in more.

options.text: **Ana** invests $2,400 a year from 25 to 35, then stops.

options.feedback: Ben puts in three times as much, but his money has much less time to compound.

bricks.prompt: Both accounts start with $1,000 and earn 7% a year. Which line is the one that compounds?

bricks.explanation: Compound interest earns interest on past interest, so it adds more each year and the line curves up. Simple interest adds the same $70 every year: a straight line.

options.text: Line A: it adds more each year

options.feedback: Steady growth means the same amount every year. That's simple interest, paid on the first $1,000 only.

options.text: Neither yet: compounding only kicks in after 20 years
options.feedback: It starts in year one; it's just small at first. By year 10, A is already ahead, $1,967 to $1,700.

challenge.prompt: You put $5,000 in an account earning 8% a year, compounded yearly. What is it worth after 3 years?
challenge.hint: Multiply by the growth factor once for each year.

options.feedback: That's simple interest: $400 a year. Each year should earn 8% on the new, larger balance.
That's after 1 year. Apply 8% growth three times.
That's 20% growth. Three years of 8% compounds to about 26%.

takeaways: Compound interest earns interest on past interest, so growth speeds up.
Each year, multiply the balance by (1 + rate).
Time matters most: starting early can beat investing more later.
